verdicts.claim: X's ranking algorithm weights replies far above likes (a reply the author replies back to is worth roughly 150x a like), and posts with off-platform links see reach cut 50-90%.
verdicts.evidence: The 150x figure is real but stale: opentweet.io states 'Author replies back to a reply: +75.0 (150x a like)', corroborated independently by techtimes.com's headline 'one reply outweighs 150 likes' (May 2026). But this scoring table comes from the 2023 leaked 'the-algorithm' code — xAI's Jan 2026 open-source release actually REDACTED the numeric engagement weights for security reasons, so '150x' is not confirmed in the current Phoenix codebase, only inferred from 2023 data treated as 'directionally accurate.' The link-penalty figure is where the claim breaks: the cited source itself (opentweet.io) says link posts saw a '30-50%' reach reduction by 2025, escalating to 'median engagement drop to zero' for non-Premium accounts as of March 2026 — not a flat '50-90%'. A separate independent A/B test (Jesse Colombo, Oct 2024, reported via ppc.land) found a 94% visibility reduction in one link-vs-no-link comparison. So the actual documented range is 30-50% (per the cited source) up to ~94%/near-total for non-Premium — '50-90%' doesn't match the source cited and glosses over how severe (near-zero) it now is for non-Premium accounts.
verdicts.corrected: Reply-weighting ~150x is what's reported, but sourced from 2023 code since xAI redacted current numeric weights in its 2026 release. Link penalty per the cited source is 30-50% (2025), escalating to near-total/zero engagement for non-Premium accounts since March 2026; one independent test found 94% reduction. Not a clean '50-90%' band as stated.

verdicts.claim: X Premium subscribers see a substantially higher reach floor than free accounts (one impressions analysis of ~18.5M posts found free accounts averaging under 95 impressions/post vs. ~640 for Premium), though this is third-party analysis, not X's own disclosed methodology.
verdicts.evidence: Direct fetch of the stated source (unfollr.com/blog/is-x-premium-worth-it) shows it does NOT contain these specific figures — it only cites 'Buffer's analysis of over 18 million posts' finding Premium gets '6-10x more impressions,' with no raw numbers given. The underlying Buffer source (buffer.com/resources/x-premium-review/), fetched directly, analyzed 18.8 million posts (not ~18.5M) and reported regular/free accounts 'typically under 100 impressions per post' vs Premium 'closer to 600' (and Premium+ over 1,550). These are close to but do not match the specific 95/640 figures in the claim, and they live on Buffer's page, not the cited unfollr.com post.
verdicts.corrected: Closest verifiable published figures (Buffer's analysis, ~18.8M posts, cited third-party not X's own methodology): free/regular accounts average under 100 impressions/post, Premium ~600, Premium+ over 1,550. The specific '95 vs 640 across ~18.5M posts' wording is not found in the stated source or its underlying citation.

verdicts.claim: The tabletop/board-game creator discovery and influence layer runs mainly through YouTube reviewers (e.g. Rahdo Runs Through), TikTok, and BoardGameGeek/Discord communities rather than X, meaning X reaches campaign creators and hardware/indie-hacker peers more than backer audiences.
verdicts.evidence: The stated source (boardgamedesigncourse.com) confirms YouTube reviewers (Rahdo, Dice Tower, Shut Up & Sit Down, Man vs Meeple) as the trusted influence layer and links to BoardGameGeek's reviewer wiki as the discovery resource, though it doesn't itself mention TikTok, Discord, or X. Cross-checking with Kickstarter's own official marketing guide and Board Game Design Lab confirms Discord/Facebook communities and TikTok as established pre-launch discovery/community channels for tabletop crowdfunding (e.g., the Quest Snakes campaign built its base via viral TikTok/Instagram/Twitter posts), with Twitter/X mentioned only generically alongside other platforms, never as a primary board-game discovery channel. The final comparative clause about X serving creators/indie-hackers more than backers is a reasonable inference from this pattern but isn't a directly sourced statement anywhere found.

verdicts.claim: Research on brands publicly engaging with negative complaints found companies that responded publicly to negative tweets saw a drop in stock price and brand-image reduction, because it draws more attention to the complaint — supporting an anonymized/composite approach over named public teardowns.
verdicts.evidence: Confirmed via two independent search passes surfacing direct extracts of the actual HBR article (hbr.org/2021/04/why-you-shouldnt-engage-with-customer-complaints-on-twitter, by Taha Havakhor, Temple Univ., and Dinesh Gauri, Univ. of Arkansas): 'the more a firm responded to complaints, the more likely it was to fall in both value and in perceived brand quality,' and engaging 'attracts more attention to their complaints, turning brands' social media pages into an area of negativity.' Matches the claim's framing precisely; the article's own recommendation is a closed (private-redirect) response strategy over an open public one, consistent with an anonymized/composite approach being favored over named public teardowns.

verdicts.claim: The clearest evidenced build-in-public-to-customers pipeline (Pieter Levels' Photo AI: $5.4K in week one, $132K MRR by month 18) converted an audience built over roughly a decade of daily posting, not a 90-day cold start — this caps how aggressively 90-day pipeline expectations should be set.
verdicts.evidence: Direct fetch of the cited gitconnected/Medium article was blocked by a redirect loop, but the $5.4K week-one and $132K-by-month-18 figures are independently corroborated across 4+ sources: Indie Hackers case study titled '$0 to $132K MRR in 18 Months,' ppc.land, working-ref.com, and founderreality.com. Multiple sources also confirm Levels had ~350,000 Twitter followers at Photo AI's Feb 2023 launch and had spent 10+ years building his overall audience (~600K+ followers), directly matching the claim's 'decade of daily posting, not a 90-day cold start' framing.

verdicts.claim: Typefully's paid tiers ($8 Starter / $19 Creator with AI writing / $39 Team) and Hypefury's tiers (from $29, sweet spot $65) both fit inside the founder's $100-150/mo total tool budget individually, but Typefully Creator is the cheaper way to get AI-assisted drafting.
verdicts.evidence: Direct fetch of typefully.com/pricing only returned nav/footer (client-side rendered pricing), so relied on consistent secondary corroboration: aiproductivity.ai, socialrails.com, checkthat.ai, xpatla.com, and comparetiers.com all independently report Typefully as Free / Starter $8 / Creator $19 (with AI writing + analytics) / Team $39 — matching the claim exactly. Hypefury pricing sources (wearefounders.uk, socialrails.com, bolta.ai) independently confirm Starter at $29/mo and Creator at $65/mo described as the 'sweet spot' tier — matching the claim. Both $19 (Typefully Creator) and $65 (Hypefury Creator) sit well within a $100-150/mo budget, and Typefully Creator ($19) is indeed cheaper than Hypefury's AI-capable tier ($65) for AI-assisted drafting.
